metadata.name: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)
metadata.summary: Bedside consciousness assessment across Eye, Verbal, and Motor responses (range 3–15).
clinical_pearls: Always record the best response observed in each domain; report E/V/M subscores alongside total.
For intubated patients, document V1T rather than guessing verbal output.
If any component is untestable (e.g., local eye edema/injury, intubation, sedation/paralysis), record it as NT rather than assigning 1 and do not sum into a total score (Teasdale et al., 2014).
Serial GCS trends over time are more accurate for prognosis and detecting deterioration than a single isolated measurement.
Pitfall — Intubation threshold: A GCS ≤ 8 signals severe obtundation requiring careful airway assessment, but should not be used in isolation without clinical context to decide intubation.
Pitfall — Simplified alternatives: Scores like the Simplified Motor Score (SMS) perform similarly for initial ED/prehospital triage, but lack the longitudinal trending validation of full GCS.

references.citation: Teasdale G, Jennett B. Assessment of coma and impaired consciousness. A practical scale. Lancet. 1974;2(7872):81-84.
Moore L, Lavoie A, Camden S, et al. Statistical validation of the Glasgow Coma Score. J Trauma. 2006;60(6):1238-1244.
Reith FC, Van den Brande R, Synnot A, Gruen R, Maas AI. The reliability of the Glasgow Coma Scale: a systematic review. Intensive Care Med. 2016;42(1):3-15.
Teasdale G, Maas A, Lecky F, Manley G, Stocchetti N, Murray G. The Glasgow Coma Scale at 40 years: standing the test of time. Lancet Neurol. 2014;13(8):844-854.

interpretation.label: Severe Consciousness Impairment (Coma)
interpretation.summary: GCS 3–8: coma range; evaluate airway protection and urgent neuroimaging.

interpretation.label: Moderate Consciousness Impairment
interpretation.summary: GCS 9–12: moderate impairment requiring close neurological monitoring.

interpretation.label: Mild / Normal Consciousness
interpretation.summary: GCS 13–15: mild impairment or normal alertness.

assessment_guides.title: Motor Response — Localizing vs Withdrawal vs Abnormal Flexion
bedside_steps: Apply fingertip pressure to the nailbed first; if no localization, apply central stimulus (supraorbital notch or trapezius squeeze).
pitfalls_and_exceptions: Localizing (M5): hand crosses the midline or rises above the clavicle toward the central stimulus.
Normal flexion (M4): rapid elbow flexion away from stimulus; Abnormal flexion (M3): slow, stereotyped adduction/flexion with wrist flexion.
